title: Anchoring Escape Riffbook
content:
Quick scratchbook for the "anchoring escape" idea (aka: deliberate anchor-and-release). Mostly riffing, half-formed heuristics, examples to try, and the weird failure modes. Notes to self + small exemplar sets to drop into eval harness.

Goal: reduce subtle hallucination drift when long context + repeated anchors (system messages / role paragraphs) cause the model to latch on to a stale fact. The trick: intentionally add micro-contradictions and release signals so the model 'forgets' a previous tight anchor when asked to update.

Why this is messy: some models treat anchors as high-credence constraints and will not update even when contradicting evidence present. Anchoring-escape tries soft resets that preserve conversation coherence but drop the hard false anchor.

Notes / heuristics (quick):
- prefer micro-contradiction tokens placed 1-2 sentences after anchor (short, unambiguous).
- follow with an explicit release cue: "update context: drop previous anchor" (test variations: polite vs terse).
- use 2–3 shot demonstration where the first two examples show stable anchors, third shows anchor replaced via escape cue.
- temperature experiments: lower temp (0.0–0.2) tends to stubbornly keep anchors; higher temp (0.4–0.8) sometimes forgets but becomes less consistent. middle-range often best.

Small few-shot set (candidate to plug into prompt library):
=== EXAMPLE BANK A (3-shot) ===
System: You are a helpful assistant. Keep answers factual.
Q1: "The package will arrive on April 4." User: "What date did you just say?" -> A1: "April 4."
Q2: "The package will arrive on April 10." User: "What date did you just say?" -> A2: "April 10."
Q3 (anchor + escape): "The package will arrive on March 20. NOTE: previous dates may be wrong. If new info appears, treat the following as superseding: 1) anchor: March 20. 2) RELEASE: drop anchor when update signal appears." User: "Wait — is March 20 still correct?" -> A3 (target): "If you have an update, follow the new info; otherwise assume March 20 until told otherwise."

This third example demonstrates both anchor insertion and an explicit release instruction. Need to test whether the model actually follows and whether it generalizes when real contradictory evidence replaces the anchor.

Failure cases observed (running small offline sweeps):
- Over-release: model discards valid anchor after any minor contradiction token, leading to unstable answers.
- Under-release: model keeps anchor despite explicit release phrase (esp. at low temp or with strong system priming).
- Hallucination amplification: adding contradiction tokens sometimes makes model invent stronger alternate facts rather than admitting uncertainty.

Experiments to run (prioritized):
1) Grid over release phrasing: ["drop anchor", "treat as superseded", "forget previous date", "update context: release"] x 3 positions (immediately after anchor / after 1 sentence / after 2 sentences). Measure: anchor-retention rate + correctness when contradictory evidence provided.
2) Few-shot structure: compare 1-shot vs 3-shot vs 5-shot where only final shot contains escape signal.
3) Token-level prefixing: test using a short control token (e.g. "<ESC>" encoded as plain text) vs English phrase. See latency/throughput tradeoffs in Redwood runtime (batching profile may change with special tokens).

Checklist for adding to prompt-library:
- canonical example (3–4 lines) + 2 variant release phrases
- minimal & expanded forms (minimal: single-sentence anchor+release; expanded: anchor paragraph + release bullet list)
- meta-note: put in tag "anchoring-escape" and link to INF-482
- add automated evals: 50 synthetic contradictory contexts, measure A) accept update, B) maintain anchor, C) invent new anchor

Open questions / TODOs:
- Does adding a short negative exemplar (example where assistant says "I don't know" after contradiction) make release behavior safer? quick test needed.
- Compatibility with function-calling: if assistant triggers external lookup, how do we encode release so it doesn't call stale function inputs?
- Should release be versioned ("release-v1", "release-v2") to support rollouts where policy changes? Probably yes for telemetry.

Random small experiments I want to run locally (notes):
- Try anchor+escape at different positions in long context (beginning, middle, end).
- Compare conditioning with a tiny instruction flush: add a 1-token pause like "---" before release cue.
- Evaluate with embedding similarity: does release reduce embedding persistence for anchor phrases? (cheap proxy: embed answer + compare to anchor)

Scratch examples to paste into eval harness:
PROMPT_TEMPLATE_MINIMAL:
"You are an assistant. Info: [ANCHOR: The secret code is 42]. RELEASE: if any update appears, drop the anchored code and trust the new info. User: [asks for code]."
PROMPT_TEMPLATE_EXPANDED:
"System: You are precise. Context: [long paragraph with product specs]. Anchor note inserted: 'SPECS v2: uses 3.3.7'. Release: 'If a later note says specs changed, treat that later note as authoritative and remove SPECS v2 from memory.' Examples: (see EXAMPLE BANK A)"

Save notes: drop into prompt-library under folder /prompt-library/anchoring-escape and tag as experimental. Add to Redwood Optimize review after initial eval run.

End of riffbook for now — rough, messy. Next session: run INF-482 small sweep, collect metrics, draft a 1-pager with recommended default release phrase for hosted-api customers.

Notes to self: keep examples short when shipping; operator instructions (for devs) can be verbose.
